summary: Learners (ages 13–14) study how recreational drugs act on the body as chemicals that change how a body SYSTEM works — framed mechanistically and non-judgementally. Core tasks: classify drugs as depressants (slow the nervous system, e.g. alcohol), stimulants (speed it up, e.g. nicotine, caffeine) or hallucinogens (distort perception); attach specific organ harms to alcohol (liver damage/cirrhosis, impaired judgement and reactions) and tobacco (lung disease and cancer, cardiovascular harm); and distinguish physical dependence (body adapts, withdrawal) from psychological dependence (craving/compulsion). A body-map reveal activity, a probing in-role dialogue, a classification check, and an optional reaction-time model each address different facets. All content must be age-appropriate, non-sensational and safeguarding-aware.
misconceptions: Thinking alcohol is a stimulant because it can make people lively — it is a depressant.
Believing dependence is only physical (missing psychological dependence/craving).
Assuming legal drugs (alcohol, tobacco) are therefore harmless.
Thinking harm is only immediate, missing long-term/cumulative organ damage.
Treating all illegal drugs as identical rather than having different classes and effects.

activities.title: Tappable body-map of drug effects with myth-busting flaps
steps: Tap an organ on a body diagram to reveal the specific effect: liver → 'alcohol is broken down here; heavy use scars it (cirrhosis)'; lungs → 'tobacco smoke damages airways and causes cancer'; brain → 'depressants slow nerve signals, stimulants speed them up'; heart → tobacco's cardiovascular harm.
Use a side panel to sort each named drug (alcohol, nicotine, caffeine, a hallucinogen) into depressant / stimulant / hallucinogen by its nervous-system effect.

Open lift-the-flap myth-busters and predict the answer before revealing: 'Is alcohol a stimulant?' → 'No — it is a depressant that slows you down, which is why it impairs reactions.' / 'Can you be dependent without physical withdrawal?' → 'Yes — psychological dependence (craving) is real.'
activities.insight: A drug is a chemical that changes how a specific body system works. It can cause short-term changes in behaviour and, for some drugs (especially with heavy or long-term use), long-term organ damage. Effects vary with the drug, the dose and the person, so drugs are not simply 'good' or 'bad'.

activities.title: In-role conversation with a GP or addiction nurse
steps: Ask an in-role GP or addiction nurse age-appropriate questions about how alcohol and tobacco affect the body, why dependence develops, and how to make safe choices.
Explain your own reasoning about a scenario (e.g. why someone might keep using a drug they know is harmful) and have it probed Socratically.
Work through why physical dependence (withdrawal symptoms) differs from psychological dependence (craving, compulsion) in a real question-and-answer exchange.
activities.insight: Behaviour, decision-making and dependence can be explored through responsive dialogue that probes a learner's reasoning, complementing the factual organ-effect core.

activities.title: Classification and drug→organ check
steps: Categorise named drugs as depressant, stimulant or hallucinogen.
Match each drug to the main organ(s) it harms (e.g. alcohol → liver/brain; tobacco → lungs/heart).
Answer items distinguishing physical from psychological dependence.
activities.insight: Secure recall of the classification and specific organ harms, and of the physical/psychological dependence distinction.

activities.title: Optional reaction-time / synapse mini-model
steps: Explore a simple model of nervous-system signal transmission where a depressant lengthens reaction time and a stimulant shortens it.
Compare the modelled reaction time for a depressant versus a stimulant and connect it to real behaviour (e.g. why alcohol impairs reactions).
activities.insight: Makes the mechanism felt: 'depressant' and 'stimulant' describe slowing or speeding of nervous-system signalling, which drives the behavioural effects.

checkQuestion: Alcohol is legal and is often described as a way to 'loosen up' and feel more confident, so some people assume it's a stimulant and basically harmless. Which category does alcohol actually belong to — depressant, stimulant, or hallucinogen — and does being legal make it safe? Explain what 'depressant' really means here.
checkAnswer: Alcohol is a depressant: it slows down the nervous system, giving slower reactions, impaired judgement and slurred speech, even though people feel less inhibited at first. 'Depressant' means it depresses (slows) nervous-system activity — not that it makes you sad. Being legal does not make it safe: alcohol causes liver damage and many deaths, and tobacco (also legal) causes lung cancer.
